title: JWST finds glassy ice in a young planetary system
freshness: Peer-reviewed research article published in Science on November 12, 2026; preferred 15-day search window.
excerpt: JWST has directly detected water and carbon-dioxide ice in the debris disk around Beta Pictoris. The water is overwhelmingly amorphous, and its broad distribution points to frequent collisions among icy planetary building blocks.
whyItMatters: The ice resembles material in Solar System comets and may preserve chemistry from before the young star finished forming. Its presence shows how collisions can keep ancient volatile ingredients visible while a planetary system is still taking shape.
whatToExploreNext: How does amorphous ice trap gases differently from crystalline ice, and what happens when that material enters a growing planet?

sources.label: Carbon dioxide and amorphous water ices in the debris disk around Beta Pictoris

body:
## Ice in a young system's rubble

JWST has found water and carbon-dioxide ice in the debris disk around Beta Pictoris, a young star 64 light-years away. This is the first direct detection of ice in that disk, despite years of indirect clues that frozen material should be there.

Beta Pictoris is about 20 million years old and already hosts three known planets. Around them stretches an edge-on disk of dust and larger fragments. It is not the gas-rich disk from which the star first formed. It is a debris disk, continually replenished as comets and planetesimals collide and grind one another down.

The outer disk is cold enough for volatile molecules to freeze. Astronomers had also detected carbon monoxide gas that ultraviolet light should destroy within only 50 to 300 years. That short lifetime suggested that collisions were releasing fresh gas from icy bodies, but earlier searches had not seen the ice itself.

## Reading reflected starlight

The team observed Beta Pictoris with JWST's Near Infrared Spectrograph, or NIRSpec. Four telescope pointings covered a region about 109 by 250 astronomical units across while avoiding the glare of the central star. One astronomical unit is the average Earth-Sun distance.

After subtracting a reference star's light pattern, the researchers measured how the disk reflected different infrared wavelengths. They extracted spectra from two regions roughly 100 astronomical units from Beta Pictoris, one on each side of the star. Both showed a broad water-ice feature near 3 micrometres and narrower carbon-dioxide features near 4.26 and 4.39 micrometres.

Those absorption fingerprints are the measured result. Models and laboratory ice spectra then helped translate their shapes and depths into composition. The inferred carbon-dioxide abundance is about 11 percent relative to water ice, close to one carbon-dioxide molecule for every nine water molecules. That sits within the ranges measured in Solar System comets and in younger planet-forming disks.

The water is also structurally unusual. Crystalline ice arranges its molecules in an ordered lattice and produces a sharp spectral peak near 3.1 micrometres. JWST did not see that peak. The smoother profile is a better match for amorphous ice, a disordered, glass-like solid that forms under very cold conditions. The models limit crystalline water to less than 7 percent of the ice volume.

## Old material, new collisions

The carbon-dioxide feature is broader and shifted relative to pure crystalline carbon-dioxide ice. A laboratory mixture containing one part carbon dioxide to ten parts amorphous water gives the closest match, though the authors cannot exclude every other mixture. The result suggests that carbon dioxide is embedded in water-rich grains rather than sitting in a separate layer of pure ice.

Amorphous water ice can preserve a record of cold beginnings. The team proposes that the mixture formed in a dense interstellar cloud or during the protostellar stage, then survived inside larger icy bodies. That origin is an inference from composition and structure, not a direct age measurement.

The ice signal is also similar across the two observed sides of the disk. A single recent impact would produce a more localized pattern. The broad distribution instead favors many smaller collisions that continually release micron-sized dirty-ice grains. Impacts in the outer disk are expected to stay below about 2 kilometres per second, slow enough that they need not turn the amorphous water crystalline.

Beta Pictoris therefore offers a view of two times at once: cold material inherited from the system's earliest stages, and present-day collisions exposing it to JWST. The same process may help carry water and carbon chemistry into planets forming around other stars.
